issues.legal_issue: A former custodian loses authority to cancel or revise an allotment after the property is acquired by the Central Government for rehabilitation.
material_facts: The appellants had received quasi-permanent allotments of land administered by the Custodian.
The appellants’ allotment had been cancelled, and they sought revision of that cancellation.
Before the revision request was decided, the Central Government issued a notification acquiring the relevant class of evacuee property.
The appellants’ land fell within the acquired property, and no managing officer or managing corporation was shown to have been appointed for it.
issues.conclusion: Following acquisition, the Custodian could not revise the earlier cancellation or otherwise deal with the property; the absence of an appointed managing officer did not restore that power.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 12(1) and 12(2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, notification extinguishes the evacuee’s interest and vests the property absolutely in the Central Government. Section 19 of that Act gives the power to cancel allotments to a managing officer or managing corporation and, by its overriding terms, prevails over the Custodian’s management powers under section 10 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950. Sections 16 and 17 concern management of the compensation pool and do not preserve the Custodian’s authority. The Court approved Bal Mukund v. The State of Punjab, I.L.R. 1957 Punj. 712.

predicates.appeal_challenges_refusal_to_revise_allo: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a refusal by a former custodian to revise a property-allotment decision.
predicates.property_acquired_for_rehabilitation: The Central Government acquired the property for the rehabilitation of displaced persons.
predicates.prior_custodian_administered_property: A custodian had administered the property before its acquisition by the Central Government.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a former custodian’s refusal to revise an allotment concerning property acquired for rehabilitation, and the custodian previously administered the property, the former custodian lacks power to cancel or revise the allotment.

issues.legal_issue: Continued-possession protection for an allottee depends on the allottee holding and possessing the property when it is acquired.
material_facts: The appellants’ land had been allotted under the applicable rehabilitation conditions.
The appellants’ allotment had been cancelled and they had lost possession before the acquisition notification was issued.
The appellants argued that the cancellation was erroneous, but the Court treated their lack of possession at acquisition as decisive.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were not entitled to continued-possession protection because they did not hold and possess the land on the date of acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, provides continued possession on the same conditions for a displaced person whose property was allotted under the specified conditions and acquired into the compensation pool. The Court held that the provision implicitly requires the displaced person to hold and possess the property immediately before acquisition; an allegedly erroneous earlier cancellation does not satisfy that requirement.

predicates.claim_for_continued_occupation_after_acq: The proceeding concerns an allottee’s claim to continue occupying property after it has been acquired for rehabilitation.
predicates.allotment_under_rehabilitation_condition: The property had been allotted to the claimant under conditions governing rehabilitation allotments.
predicates.in_possession_at_acquisition: The claimant held and possessed the property immediately before its acquisition.

issues.definition: An allottee who claims continued occupation after acquisition under rehabilitation allotment conditions is not entitled to that protection if the allottee was not in possession when the property was acquired.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction on transferring property during specified pending proceedings does not bar a quasi-permanent allotment when the transfer is not a final compensation settlement and the pending proceeding is before an authority under the earlier property regime.
material_facts: A proceeding concerning the appellants’ quasi-permanent allotment was pending before an authority established under the earlier evacuee-property regime.
The disputed transfer concerned a quasi-permanent allotment, not a final transfer in settlement of a compensation claim.
The appellants relied on a rule concerning property that was the subject of a pending case.
issues.conclusion: The rule did not prevent the allotment because it governed transfers by way of final settlement of compensation claims and applied to proceedings before authorities established under the later rehabilitation regime.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 74 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, appears in the chapter dealing with payment of compensation under section 10 and concerns transfer of property to an allottee as final settlement of a compensation claim. It does not govern quasi-permanent allotments or proceedings before authorities created under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_quasi_permanent_al: The proceeding concerns a challenge to a quasi-permanent allotment of property.
predicates.transfer_is_not_final_compensation_settl: The proposed transfer is not a final settlement of a displaced person’s compensation claim.
predicates.pending_case_is_before_legacy_property_a: The pending case is before an authority established under the earlier evacuee-property regime.

issues.definition: A restriction directed to final compensation-settlement transfers does not bar a quasi-permanent allotment when the pending case is before an authority under the earlier property regime.
